newsitem.title: USA: Labor markets seen tight in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Labor markets seen tight in 1997.

text.p: The job market is likely to stay tight next year as moderate economic growth keeps demand for workers keen, economists and a former Federal Reserve official said.
"We're going to have a tight labour market next year," said Preston Martin, a former Fed vice-chairman who is chairman of Home Vest Financial Services Inc.

The unemployment rate is expected to average 5.3 percent in 1997, according to forecasts from 11 economists at major brokerage houses and banks compiled by PSA The Bond Market Trade Association. The unemployment rate stood at 5.4 percent in November.

Private analysts predicted that the economy will create 150,000 to 175,000 news jobs a month in 1997 on average, slightly slower than the 205,000 created each month outside the farm sector through November 1996.
Analysts said demand for workers would vary depending on industry and type of business.
Certain sectors, notably those requiring highly skilled workers, are likely to have a harder time trying to hire as those workers are in scarce supply, analysts said.
High-technology, for example, is one of the sectors most affected by a shortage of workers.

Analysts said some businesses have been unable to find enough workers for things such as computer security tasks, a trend that could gain momentum as the Internet's commercial potential is more fully exploited.
Labour experts estimate, for example, that no more than 200 supercomputer security experts currently work in this country, and most of them are not available for hire.
"The skills that are demanded for certain professionals ... are disproportionate to other things going on in the economy," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank.
That suggests employers will have to create training programmes for new workers or hire them from other companies. Either way, experts said, wage costs were expected to rise.
Non-skilled labour is also seen tight in 1997, though not as much so.

Richard Rippe, chief economist at Prudential Securities Inc., said he has detected some tightness even in the entry-level job market. "Labor costs (in general) will rise a little bit in 1997," Rippe said.
So what kind of impact will all this have on inflation?

"I personally think you'll see inflation drift up a little bit (in 1997). But it's still a very gradual process. We don't have such a tight labour market that we're going to see inflation rising quickly," said William Dudley, chief economist at Goldman Sachs & Co.
Some analysts said tight labour markets would lead to higher inflation but others weren't so sure.
Rather than companies raising prices because of higher labour costs, some suggested that higher wages might fuel enough demand to eventually justify companies' price increases.
"I think inflation will be more demand-driven (in 1997)," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
"I can see it happening in things that I buy. It's very slow, almost imperceptible but I can start to see it."
But he and others noted that competitive pressures were likely to keep price increases in check.
Analysts expect the economy overall to growth about 2 percent to 2.25 percent in 1997, what economists consider an ideal long-term growth rate that will not fuel inflation.
